attachments.name: 2025-033 RESO Approving Code Lien Amnesty Program
Lien Amnesty Programs - Municipal and County Comparisons
Lien Amnesty Program - St. Lucie County

description:
The City's code compliance unit processes are governed by FSS 162, Chapter 2 - Article III - Division 2 of our City's Code of Ordinances and department policy. These processes see officers issue Notices of Violation when violations of the City’s Code of Ordinances and Florida Building Code are identified, and violations not corrected within the required time are presented to, and ruled on, by the Special Magistrate. When compliance is not achieved in the timeframe ordered by the Special Magistrate, code liens are placed on properties within the City's jurisdiction. As of April 2, 2025, and pursuant to orders issued by our Magistrates, our City has 124 code liens attached to non-homesteaded properties due to unresolved code cases, and unpaid fines and fees. The total amount of these liens is $9,699,560.00. Our City currently has 35 homesteaded properties with liens, totaling $2,930,625.00. The grand total amount of these liens was $12,630,185.00.
In an effort to encourage voluntary compliance and resolve long-standing code enforcement liens, the City of Wilton Manors endeavors to implement a Lien Amnesty Program. The program is intended to provide eligible property owners a limited-time opportunity to apply for a reduction of accrued fines (excluding administrative fees) associated with code enforcement violations.
City staff designed the below policy components based on discussions at the Commission's January 28, 2025 Commission Meeting, and additional discussion via individual emails and one-on-one conversations. This proposed policy provides clear program standards for applicants to understand, and for staff to process and manage. We ask the Commission to finalize a policy as they so desire.
AMNESTY PERIOD
The Lien Amnesty Program shall be in effect from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026. During this period, eligible property owners may apply for a reduction in fines. One will be eligible for amnesty consideration if their application and non-refundable application fee payment is received by the City within this timeframe.
REDUCTION CONSIDERATIONS AND PAYMENT
The following reductions shall be administered as authorized by the City Commission:
July 1, 2025 – March 31, 2026
Homesteaded Properties: 90 %
Non-Homesteaded Properties: 80 %
April 1, 2026 – June 30, 2026
Homesteaded Properties: 80%
Non-Homesteaded Properties: 70%
The date an application and application fee is received by the City determines the reduction amount. Any reduction granted shall be contingent upon payment to the City within ninety (90) calendar days from the time the City provides written notice of approval to the property owner. If the ninetieth day falls on a day the City is closed, payment shall be made the first day the City is open. Failure to pay within the required time shall result in reinstatement of the original lien amount, and the property becoming ineligible for the program.
ELIGIBILITY
In order to be eligible for the Lien Amnesty Program, applicants shall meet the following criteria:The property must be located within the jurisdiction of the City of Wilton Manors.
Homesteaded and non-homesteaded properties are eligible.
The applicant must be the current owner of record for the property up through and including the date the lien is satisfied. The source for verification of ownership is the Broward County Property Appraiser (BCPA) records;
The source for verification of ownership if a property is listed under a corporation is the State of Florida Division of Corporations; i. The applicant shall be listed as a registered agent or authorized person.
Property owners with multiple code liens on a property shall apply for a reduction of each lien on the property simultaneously under the Lien Amnesty Program;
The property shall be in compliance with the City’s Code;Any and all violations on the property shall be complied prior to applying; and
No application shall be processed unless and until a code compliance officer verifies the subject property is in compliance with the City’s Code.
Property owners shall not have active violations on any property they own in the City;
Property owners shall not have any outstanding real estate taxes or other sums due to the City;
Each lien shall have a minimum face value of $1,000.00 and must not have been under an Order of Reduction by the Special Magistrate or City Commission;
Eligible liens shall not exceed a total face value of $250,000 at the time the application is submitted;
Should an application be submitted and then found by the City not to meet the minimum standards for submission, the application shall be rejected with written notice provided to the applicant. The applicant may reapply once the minimum standards have been met.
The following liens and fines are not eligible for the Lien Amnesty Program:Liens arising from Unsafe Structures Board actions and orders;
Liens arising from abatement actions, including but not limited to nuisance abatement, are not eligible until all code violations have been complied, and the City has been paid in full for costs incurred to abate violations;
Liens arising from the Building Safety Inspection Program are not eligible until all requirements of the Building Safety Inspection Program are satisfied, including but not limited to required repairs;
Liens resulting from repeat violations are not eligible;
Fines imposed for dog bites and solid waste franchise violations are not eligible;
Utility liens are not eligible; and
Liens the City has taken foreclosure action against in County court at the direction of the City Commission. Once the City Commission provides official approval for the City to seek foreclosure action, any associated liens shall become ineligible for this program.
APPLICATION / APPLICATION AND LIEN RELEASE FEES
Eligible property owners shall submit a formal application to the City during the amnesty period, and as directed by the City. A non-refundable application fee payment in the amount of $200.00 that covers total costs associated with processing individual requests for lien amnesty shall be submitted with the application. A non-refundable release of lien fee in the amount of $415.00 shall be submitted to the City prior to the City releasing any lien.
APPEALS
The City’s lien amnesty program shall have no appeal process, and the determination by the Chief of Police or department designee to approve or reject requests for lien amnesty shall become final.

description:
The City currently utilizes BS&A’s cloud-based solutions for various municipal functions. To enhance efficiency and streamline operations within Community Development Services, Police and Leisure Services Departments, staff proposes the addition of the BS&A Community Development Module. This module will provide comprehensive automation and modernization of key city processes, ensuring improved constituent services and operational effectiveness. The proposed module includes the following components:
Building, Permits, and Inspections
Planning, Zoning, and Engineering
Code Enforcement
Business Licensing
BS&A Online Services – Inspections
BS&A Online Services – Permit Applications
Special Event Permit Application and Processing
This robust solution is designed to empower the city with role-based, flexible automation tools. Key benefits include quick implementation, advanced analytics, constituent self-service capabilities, and GIS integration to support informed decision-making. The inclusion of Special Event Permit Application and Processing will specifically streamline and automate workflows within the Leisure Services Department, improving interdepartmental coordination and service delivery. The addition of BS&A’s Community Development Module aligns with the city’s commitment to modernization and efficiency. The cost savings and improved service delivery justify the investment, making this module a valuable enhancement to the city’s existing cloud-based solutions.

description:
The City entered into an agreement with SaferWatch, LLC on October 1, 2019, which expired on September 30, 2024. The Wilton Manors Police Department requests approval from the City Commission to continue procuring services from SaferWatch, LLC in order to ensure operational efficiency, maintain compatibility and achieve cost savings now and in the future.
Approval of the new software agreement will allow the City to continue utilizing SaferWatch's services to meet our public safety needs. Through the SaferWatch mobile app, residents, visitors, students, teachers, and staff have a direct, real-time connection to the Wilton Manors Police Department.
The SaferWatch platform enables individuals to report incidents, receive safety alerts, and engage in two-way communication with law enforcement. The service is trusted by other reputable agencies, such as the Broward County School Board, Broward Sheriff's Office, Fort Lauderdale Police Department, and other local police departments. SaferWatch offers software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools, including a secure web portal (the "Command Center"), and other related services designed for both emergency and non-emergency situations, as well as the reporting of tips and information.
The Agreement will remain in effect until either party provides written notice of termination, in accordance with the terms outlined therein.

attachments.name: 2025-031 RESO Approving ILA with Broward County for Participation in the RIR Program exp. 2030
ILA with Broward County Participation Residential Irrigation Rebate Program - Naturescape Irrigation Service
Residential Irrigation Rebate program ILA with County exp. 9-30-2030

description:
On March 26, 2024, the City Commission approved participation in the Broward County Residential Irrigation Rebate (RIR) Program through an interlocal agreement. The RIR Program offers rebates of up to $600 to residents who upgrade their irrigation systems to conserve water and energy. The program is only open to residences on city water, and residences with wells are not eligible. More information can be found at the City's RIR web page.
The County's practice is to pass a blanket, five year Interlocal Agreement for all participating cities. That five year ILA expired March 30, 2025, so the new agreement will be for the term of April 2025 through March 2030.
Year One is for a period of 18 months (April 2025 through September 2026), to get the program on a fiscal year frequency, so the commitment is increased to account for that factor. The County also offers a Naturescape Irrigation (NIS) Program, which provides the same service to city facilities, but the City is not opting in to NIS at this time.
The City appropriated $5,000 for the program, and the funds were completely utilized in the first quarter of the year. There is currently a "wait list" of approximately six residences who wish to participate. The City Commission recently approved Resolution 2025-021, which provided for an additional $5,000, to bring the City's annual commitment to $10,000 in rebates and approximately $5,000 in administrative costs.

description:
During the February 11, 2025 City Commission meeting, the City Manager requested clarification of topics for an upcoming workshop based on a re-evaluation of Article 030 of the City's Unified Land Development Regulations as stated in one of the City's Strategic goals. Those topics include the evaluation of maximum height; rezoning of Transit Oriented Corridor West (TOC-W) to bifurcate parcels adjacent to Andrews Avenue from the parcels adjacent to Oakland Park Boulevard and the creation of a new zoning district; rezoning of parcels adjacent to Colohatchee Park to Transit Oriented Corridor East (TOC-E); an evaluation of dimensional requirements and the required number of parking spaces; consideration of additional types of parking spaces; setbacks; the minimum square footage of a dwelling unit; and rental conversions as it relates to height incentives for affordable housing. Based on discussion with the City Commission, City staff was directed to provide an estimate of the time and cost that would be required for City staff to evaluate and process the requested changes to Article 30 of the City's ULDRs. The costs associated with each project take into consideration the various tasks for completion, which include, but are not limited to, consulting fees, posting of large public hearing/notice signs, advertisements, mailings and staff time.
At the March 11, 2025, City Commission Meeting, City staff was directed to schedule one (1) Article 030 re-evaluation item at a time for discussion in lieu of scheduling a City Commission workshop. The first discussion item with the City Commission on April 8, 2025 was an evaluation of dimensional requirements and the required number of parking spaces, and consideration of additional types of parking spaces. The second discussion item identified by the City Commission was maximum building heights.
Background: On August 24, 2021, the City Commission adopted Ordinance No. 2021-011 which included the absolute maximum height for the Urban Center Mixed Use zoning districts. Section 030-038 provides the absolute maximum height (allowable base height plus additional incentive height) within the Urban Center Mixed Use zoning districts.
City staff have provided, as part of this agenda item, the following:• Height map
• Description of maximum heights
In addition, the estimations below would include processing of amendments to the City’s Unified Land Development Regulations for the evaluation of maximum height.• This task involves the analysis, recommendation, and processing of amendments to maximum heights within the Urban Center Mixed Use Zoning Districts this would include newly created TOC-W zoning district and the parcels newly rezoned to TOC-E.

description:
During the 2nd CDBG Public Hearing on March 25, 2025, the City Commission determined that lighting improvements at Mickel Park would best meet the CDBG criteria and serve a community need.
Additional background information:
The City's anticipated allocation of Community Block Grant dollars for the 51st year funding cycle is approximately $75,000. However, this amount is not guaranteed. As the Commission is aware, the primary objective of CDBG funds is to assist low to moderate income persons or neighborhoods to improve their quality of life. This may be achieved by development of social programs or through infrastructure improvements.
CDBG funds have been utilized in the past to rebuild a lift station, construct sidewalks and a drainage system, and resurface streets in the Highland Estates neighborhood. Funds have also been utilized to construct estate style fencing, the installation of an emergency generator, construction of a floating dock, the construction of an addition to the community center building, installation of an artificial turf surface on the playground and a shade structure on the rear deck, the installation of outdoor physical fitness stations, a shade structure over the fitness stations, the expansion of the basketball court and improvements to an adjacent pavilion and the installation of security cameras at Island City Park Preserve (ICPP). Funds have also been used for the construction of a facility maintenance building at Mickel Park, drainage improvements on the west side, and new LED lighting at Hagen Park.
It was suggested at previous public hearings that consideration be given to the development of programs to benefit low income residents including possible computer training programs. Unfortunately, Broward County has advised the City that no new social service programs may be funded with 49th year allocations. This is due to the limitation by HUD regulations that such programs may not exceed fifteen percent of the total allocations to all cities throughout the county. Existing programs already meet that maximum allowed level and in fact, due to the substantial reduction in funding to all the cities, some existing social service programs have had to be cut back to stay within the fifteen percent cap.
Staff received project input at two public hearings, advisory board meetings, and discussions with neighborhood associations. Projects recommended included the installation of check valves on existing stormwater outflow structures, fencing at Donn Eisele park, flashing LED lights on stop signs and construction of project recommendations in the West Side Traffic Study.

description:

Per Article 100 of the City's Unified Land Development Regulations, the Planning and Zoning Board shall hold its public hearing and shall, after reviewing the application, staff recommendation and public input, if any, make a recommendation upon the application to the City Commission of approval, denial, or approval with stipulations, based upon its consideration of the consistency of the application with the Comprehensive Plan. The proposed zoning designation of RD-10 is consistent with the underlying land use designation of R-L/MD (Low Medium 10 Residential). The R-L/MD land use designation permits up to ten (10) dwelling units per gross acre. The land use designation of the subject parcel permits up to three (3) dwelling units for a 0.344 gross acre parcel. The proposed duplex (two (2) units) is consistent with the R-L/MD land use designation. Zoning Application Z 24-02 is consistent with the goals, objectives and policies of the City of Wilton Manors Comprehensive Plan.
The first reading for Zoning Application Z 24-02 was heard by the City Commission on January 28, 2025. The zoning application was approved on first reading with the condition that the applicant must install a ten (10) foot-high hedge along the rear property line. The language regarding the additional landscaping requirement was added to the proposed ordinance.

description:
During the February 11, 2025, City Commission meeting, the City Manager requested clarification of topics for an upcoming workshop based on a re-evaluation of Article 030 of the City's Unified Land Development Regulations as stated in one of the City's Strategic goals. Those topics include the evaluation of maximum height; rezoning of Transit Oriented Corridor West (TOC-W) to bifurcate parcels adjacent to Andrews Avenue from the parcels adjacent to Oakland Park Boulevard and the creation of a new zoning district; rezoning of parcels adjacent to Colohatchee Park to Transit Oriented Corridor East (TOC-E); an evaluation of dimensional requirements and the required number of parking spaces; consideration of additional types of parking spaces; setbacks; the minimum square footage of a dwelling unit; and rental conversions as it relates to height incentives for affordable housing. Based on discussion with the City Commission, City staff was directed to provide an estimate of the time and cost that would be required for City staff to evaluate and process the requested changes to Article 30 of the City's ULDRs. The costs associated with each project take into consideration the various tasks for completion, which include, but are not limited to, consulting fees, posting of large public hearing/notice signs, advertisements, mailings and staff time.
At the March 11, 2025, City Commission Meeting, City staff was directed to schedule one (1) Article 030 re-evaluation item at a time for discussion in lieu of scheduling a City Commission workshop. The first discussion item suggested by the City Commission was an evaluation of dimensional requirements and the required number of parking spaces, and consideration of additional types of parking spaces. This task is an update to existing research Community Development Services staff has already conducted and consisting of updating research on parking space dimensions, number of parking spaces required based on use and types of parking spaces (compact, motorcycle, as examples). In addition, the estimations below would include processing of amendments to the City’s Unified Land Development Regulations.

City Attorney- 3 hours

Complete Comp Plan Amend Transmittal Package Wilton Manors (1,000 UNITS, 2 FOR 1, AND PROP RIGHTS)

description:
On August 23, 2022, the City Commission of the City of Wilton Manors voted to transmit a proposed amendment to the City of Wilton Manors’ Comprehensive Plan (Ordinance No. 2022-015) that included the request to 1) add 1,000 dwelling units within the Transit Oriented Corridor (TOC) land use designation, 2) allow for double the maximum number of dwelling units for hotel units and Special Residential Facility Category (3) development which would equate to two (2) sleeping rooms to be equal to one (1) dwelling unit; 3) and the addition of a Property Rights Element. The proposed comprehensive plan amendment was transmitted to the State on September 1, 2022, and to the Broward County Planning Council on October 4, 2022. As part of the Broward County Planning Council’s review of the proposed amendment, the application was sent to the City of Fort Lauderdale as an adjacent City. On December 6, 2022, the City of Fort Lauderdale retracted the City of Wilton Manors’ Water and Wastewater Available Capacity letter (dated June 17, 2022) and subsequently the proposed comprehensive plan amendment was placed on hold until the water and wastewater capacity issue was resolved.
On May 16, 2024, the City of Wilton Manors received a letter from the City of Fort Lauderdale granting water and wastewater capacity for 1,000 dwelling units. In lieu of continuing with the proposed land use plan amendment to allow for an additional 1,000 dwelling units in the TOC land use designation, the City applied to the Broward County Planning Council for 750 redevelopment units. The City Commission authorized the request for 750 redevelopment units to Broward County Planning Council via Resolution 2024-076 which was adopted on July 23, 2024. The application for redevelopment units was approved by the Broward County Board of County Commissioners on December 10, 2024.
Dependent upon direction from the City Commission, City staff will work with the City Attorney to determine what process is required to eliminate the request for 1,000 additional units from Ordinance No. 2022-015. If the City Commission wishes to proceed with the remainder of the pending comprehensive plan amendment application, the amendment will require two (2) transmittals to the State (one after the first reading by the City Commission and then one after the second reading by the City Commission). Once, the proposed amendment is adopted by the City Commission and transmitted to the State, the City’s Comprehensive Plan as amended must be recertified by the Broward County Planning Council. The adoption of the proposed amendment must be conditional upon approval of the recertification of the Broward County Planning Council. Section 163.3177(6)(i)2, Florida Statutes (Chapter 2021-195, Laws of Florida) requires the City to adopt and include a Property Rights Element into their comprehensive plan. The Property Rights Element must be adopted prior to “any” future plan amendment.
title: Land Use Plan Amendment / Comprehensive Plan (LUPA) update

description:
The City’s anticipated allocation of Community Block Grant dollars for the 51st year funding cycle (2025/2026) is estimated at $76,000. The primary objective of CDBG funds is to assist low to moderate income persons or neighborhoods to improve their quality of life. This may be achieved by developing social programs or through infrastructure improvements. According to the socio-economic data collected by the county, the eligible neighborhoods in Wilton Manors for capital or infrastructure improvements are in the southwest and south central areas in the City.
CDBG funds have been utilized in the past to re-build the sewage lift station, construct sidewalks and a drainage system, and resurface streets in the Highland Estates neighborhood. Funds have also been utilized to improve Island City Park Preserve, including the construction or installation of estate style fencing, an emergency generator, a 35-foot floating dock, an addition to the community center building, an artificial turf surface on the playground, a shade structure on the rear deck, fitness station, a shade structure over the fitness station, a basketball court renovation, and security cameras. Funds have also been utilized to acquire and develop the property adjacent to ICPP at 811 N.E. 28th Street. More recently, funds were allocated for improvements to the existing ball field and a new storage and maintenance facility building at Mickel Park and drainage improvements on the west side of the City. The first phase of energy efficient lighting installations at Hagen Park (48th year) was recently completed.
Broward County has advised that no new social service programs, such as possible computer training, will be funded with 51st year allocations. This is due to the limitation by HUD regulations that such programs may not exceed fifteen percent of the total allocations to all cities through the county. Existing programs already meet that maximum allowed level and, in fact, due to the substantial reduction in funding to all the cities, some existing social service programs have had to be cut back to stay within the fifteen percent cap.
This public hearing provides an opportunity to receive input from residents. Staff has reached out to the neighborhood associations for input. This is the second public meeting being held for the 51st Year CDBG program. At the conclusion of this meeting, City Staff will present a project for Commission approval based on the public input and the parameters of the grant application.
title: Public Hearing to discuss potential CDBG 51st Year Projects

description:
This resolution authorizes staff to engage a professional consulting firm to update the City’s Utility Rate Study (study) and develop a financial model capable of evaluating alternatives to generate the necessary funding to repay the upcoming WIFIA debt service annually. This study will ensure that the city’s utility rates remain equitable and sufficient to meet operational, capital, and debt service needs.
The firm of Raftelis Financial Consultants, Inc. (Raftelis), which conducted the 2021 utility rate study, has been selected to perform the study update. Their familiarity with the city’s financial structure and historical data will provide continuity and efficiency in analyzing trends and making necessary adjustments. This study will provide transparency and public engagement opportunities to ensure community input on potential rate adjustments and funding strategies. A periodic update of the utility rate study is essential to maintain fiscal responsibility and ensure rates remain fair for residents and businesses.
By engaging Raftelis, the city will benefit from expert analysis and industry best practices to develop a comprehensive financial strategy for utility operations.

description:
The Wilton Manors Police Department is seeking approval from the City Commission to enter into an agreement with PowerDMS, which is a Public Safety solution subsidiary of NEOGOV. PowerDMS is document management software that the Police Department has utilized since its approval by the Commission in 2015, in accordance with its participation agreement.
Prior to implementing PowerDMS, the accreditation process relied on paper documents, making the dissemination of directives and other critical materials a manual and time-consuming process. This often resulted in delays, inconsistencies, and challenges in tracking compliance and updates.
PowerDMS is a compliance requirement for accreditation and is used by law enforcement officers to meet the minimum mandatory policy review and training requirements necessary to maintain Florida Department of Law Enforcement certification. The Police Department seeks to continue its professional partnership with PowerDMS, which has been in place for over ten (10) years.
The agreement will remain in effect until either party provides written notice of termination, as outlined in the terms of the agreement.

description:
The Wilton Manors Stonewall Pride Parade & Street Festival, organized for the ninth consecutive year by Stonewall Pride I, Inc., will take place on Saturday, June 14, 2025. The event has historically attracted up to 50,000 attendees, generating significant local and regional economic impact. Economic studies conducted in 2017 and 2022 indicate that the event contributed $9.4 million to the regional economy in 2022.
In preparation for this significant event, City staff engaged in regular meetings with stakeholders to provide guidance, facilitate communication, and ensure the safety and seamless management of the event. The City has committed to funding a portion of the road closure costs, up to $10,000. Additionally, the City will extend support by covering staff expenses for permits and addressing logistical requirements for the special event. Building permit fees from the City will be waived, and Stonewall Pride I, Inc will cover only the direct costs associated with plan reviews and inspections, estimated at $2,500. Stonewall Pride I, Inc is requesting a waiver of staff costs related to inquiries, committee meetings, and assistance with designing the site plan layout, amounting to an estimated $3,000. However, Stonewall Pride I, Inc will bear specific staff costs related to the event, including Police Detail, Fire Watch, monitoring City facilities, and direct City staff assistance leading up to and during the event.
Stonewall Pride I, Inc is also seeking the City's cooperation in waiving regular parking fees and enforcement on the day of the event, with a request to donate all net revenues from event parking.
title: Motion to approve special event permit for Stonewall Festival and Parade.

description:
Section 010-030, “Terms defined” of the City of Wilton Manors Unified Land Development Regulations (ULDRs) contains definitions pertinent to the City’s ULDRs. Based on proposed changes to Section 030-030 of the City’s ULDRs related to permitted and prohibited uses, additional terms are required to be defined in Section 010-030 of the City’s ULDRs. Section 030-030 of the City’s ULDRs, lists the permitted and prohibited uses with the Urban Center Mixed Use Zoning Districts which includes the Wilton Drive Arts and Entertainment District (WDAE), Transit Oriented Corridor North District (TCO-N), Transit Oriented Corridor South (TOC-S), Transit Oriented Corridor East (TOC-E), and the Transit Oriented Corridor West (TOC-W) Zoning Districts. City staff proposes revisions, deletions, and additions to the permitted and prohibited use table along with specific use provisions.
The first reading of the proposed amendments was discussed during the February 11, 2025 City Commission meeting. Based upon this discussion, the following are proposed changes to Ordinance No. 2025-002:
• Reference to Chapter 10 and Code of Ordinances was added to the definition of “Adult entertainment establishment”.
• Language was added to the definition of “Pop-up” to clarify that the proposed use of the pop-up must be a permitted use within the corresponding zoning district.
• Definition of “Restaurant, fast food” was deleted and specific use provision associated with definition was also deleted.
• Definition of “Water vehicle” was added.
• Language requiring a local business tax receipt for “Food and/or beverage cart/truck” was deleted and replaced with “any food and/or beverage cart/truck that is operated on the same premises as and by a separately licensed public food service establishment may operate during the same house of operation as the separately licensed public food service establishment that operates such food and/or beverage cart/truck”.
An additional item that staff would like to discuss with the City Commission is activities that are categorized of adult entertainment establishments.

description:
The City's application for the replacement of lighting at Hagen Park was approved by the County. The City has been awarded $120,000 in 49th Year Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding for the replacement of sports lighting at Hagen Park. In addition, $200,000 has been allocated in the current fiscal year for this project. Below are the two funding allocation options for this project.
The first option is to use the existing CDBG funding to replace the lighting on the four hard tennis courts only. The estimated cost for this project ranges from $150,000 to $175,000, meaning the grant funding would cover all or most of the expense. This option provides immediate improvements to lighting conditions for the hard courts while requiring little to no additional City funding. However, it leaves the lighting for the clay courts and volleyball court unchanged, meaning the City would need to complete additional phases in the future. Delaying these additional upgrades could result in increased costs due to inflation and require additional mobilization expenses for contractors, ultimately making the overall project more expensive over time. Additionally, keeping the aging metal halide fixtures on the remaining courts and volleyball area would result in continued higher maintenance and energy costs.
The second option is to complete the full lighting replacement together by upgrading the lighting for all six tennis courts (hard and clay) and the sand volleyball court. The estimated cost for this comprehensive approach is $245,000 to $275,000, requiring the use of both CDBG and budgeted City capital funds. By purchasing the light fixtures separately with City funds and using the CDBG funding for installation, the City would avoid sales tax and reduce the overall project cost. This option also ensures that all courts are upgraded at once, eliminating the need for future mobilization costs and maximizing long-term financial benefits. In addition, replacing all aging fixtures with LED lighting provides substantial cost savings over time, including reduced energy consumption, lower maintenance expenses, and protection against rising costs due to inflation.Energy Efficiency Savings: The existing metal halide lights consume 48.4 kW, while the proposed LED system will consume only 14.56 kW, reducing energy consumption by 70%. Based on current FPL rates, this reduction translates to an estimated savings of $659 per month or $7,911 per year in electricity costs, totaling approximately $79,112 over 10 years.
Maintenance Savings: Over the past several years, the City has spent an average of $7,398 per year on repairs and maintenance to the aging lighting system. The new LED fixtures come with a 10-year warranty, which is expected to eliminate these maintenance costs, resulting in an estimated savings of $73,976 over 10 years.
Inflation & Delayed Installation Impact: If the City waits to complete the remaining courts in a later phase, inflation and rising labor costs are projected to increase the total installation price from $120,000 to an estimated $126,814 by 2027.
Lost Savings Due to Delay: If the City waits two years to complete the lighting upgrade, it will forgo an estimated $30,618 in combined energy and maintenance savings during that period. When factoring in the impact of inflation, the total financial impact of delaying the project is estimated at $37,432.

description:
At the request of the City Commission, staff reviewed the current travel policy, specifically the per diem rate. The City Commission expressed concern that the current per diem rate at $48 per day is insufficient to cover the actual cost of meals while traveling on official business. This rate has not been adjusted to reflect the rising cost of meals and travel-related expenses since 2017. Staff recommend increasing the per diem rate from $48 to $80 per day. The proposed increase aligns with the current per diem rate established by the State, ensuring consistency with industry standards. The adjustment reflects the increased cost of meals, helping to ensure that City employees and officials are not unduly burdened while conducting official City business.
The resolution also authorizes the City Manager to approve all budgeted travel and authorizes her to approve un-budgeted travel in amounts up to $1,500 as long as funds are available. Un-budgetd travel of over $1,500 will require approval by the City Commission. The current practice of notifying the City Commission of all travel in the Weekly Update will continue. The resolution also authorizes the City Manager to revise travel forms required to implement the resolution.

attachments.name: 2025-012 RESO Approving Agmt with Inliner Solutions, LLC to provide CIPP lining for LS 6
Contract Agreement w. Inliner Solutions for LS-6 Sanitary CIPP (Casselberry piggyback)

description:
The City of Wilton Manors has a current and ongoing need for sanitary sewer infrastructure maintenance and upgrades throughout the City. Specific projects have been identified in the 2020 Water, Wastewater & Stormwater Integrated Master Plan (Plan) which includes lining sewer main lines to reduce infiltration of groundwater. Infiltration occurs when water seeps into gravity-flow sanitary sewer pipelines through cracks and deteriorated joint seals, which results in increased flow volume through the system being pumped to the G.T. Lohmeyer Wastewater Treatment Plant.
In keeping with the Plan program, the City has identified Lift Station #6 (LS-6) Basin for the next lining project. The first of two steps in the Cast-In-Place-Pipe (CIPP) lining process is pressure cleaning of the sewer mains in conjunction with video recordings (Clean & TV) which reveals leaks and cracks in the system. This process has been completed for LS-6 and specific pipe sections have been identified for CIPP lining, which is the second step in the process. Inliner Solutions, LLC has proposed to CIPP line 7,553 LF in LS-6 for a cost of $408, 760.00, based on a piggyback agreement from the City of Casselberry, FL.
Lining sewer mains are expected to reduce pump run-times and reduce lift station maintenance costs. Additionally, the reduced flow will bring our system closer in line with lower design capacity levels. This is the last of the City's twelve (12) basins to receive the necessary inspection and lining since 2021. Future gravity main projects will include periodic re-inspections and maintenance as required.

description:
The City’s anticipated allocation of Community Block Grant dollars for the 51st year funding cycle (2025/2026) is estimated at $76,000. The primary objective of CDBG funds is to assist low to moderate income persons or neighborhoods to improve their quality of life. This may be achieved by developing social programs or through infrastructure improvements. According to the socio-economic data collected by the county, the eligible neighborhoods in Wilton Manors for capital or infrastructure improvements are in the southwest and south central areas in the City.
CDBG funds have been utilized in the past to re-build the sewage lift station, construct sidewalks and a drainage system, and resurface streets in the Highland Estates neighborhood. Funds have also been utilized to improve Island City Park Preserve, including the construction or installation of estate style fencing, an emergency generator, a 35-foot floating dock, an addition to the community center building, an artificial turf surface on the playground, a shade structure on the rear deck, fitness station, a shade structure over the fitness station, a basketball court renovation, and security cameras. Funds have also been utilized to acquire and develop the property adjacent to ICPP at 811 N.E. 28th Street. More recently, funds were allocated for improvements to the existing ball field and a new storage and maintenance facility building at Mickel Park and drainage improvements on the west side of the City. The first phase of energy efficient lighting installations at Hagen Park (48th year) was recently completed.
Broward County has advised that no new social service programs, such as possible computer training, will be funded with 51st year allocations. This is due to the limitation by HUD regulations that such programs may not exceed fifteen percent of the total allocations to all cities through the county. Existing programs already meet that maximum allowed level and, in fact, due to the substantial reduction in funding to all the cities, some existing social service programs have had to be cut back to stay within the fifteen percent cap.
This public hearing provides an opportunity to receive input from residents. This is the first public meeting being held for the 51st Year CDBG program. At the conclusion of the second public meeting, held at a future Commission meeting, City Staff will present a project for Commission approval based on the public input and the parameters of the grant application.
title: Public Hearing for the CDBG 51st Year Projects

attachments.name: 2025-014 RESO Approving David Mancini & Sons, Inc. Invoice
David Mancini & Sons Invoice - LS-11 Force Main Repair

description:
On Wednesday, August 28, 2024, the Emergency Management/Utilities office received a call at 1:30 PM stating that there was a break on the Lift Station #11 force main pipe (LS-11 FM). Utilities staff responded to the properties located at 2624 and 2632 NE 16 Ave. Upon arrival, the crew assessed the issue and confirmed that, in fact, the 1960s 16-inch sewer force main, which conveys all the raw sewage from Wilton Manors to the City of Fort Lauderdale for treatment, was broken. Staff's initial response was to reduce system-wide flow by limiting and/or stopping pump flows at all twelve of the City’s lift stations. During this time, the City of Fort Lauderdale Public Works was contacted to seek assistance with this emergency sewer break. Their recommendation was to contact David Mancini & Sons (DMS) with whom Fort Lauderdale has a contract for similar issues in their city.
DMS promptly responded to the site, and was able to deploy equipment and labor to replace the ruptured section of pipe, which was completed and back in service at 3:00 AM on August 29th. At that time, all lift stations were turned back on to relieve the major surcharge in the system. The invoice from DMS amounted to $62,659.75. Staff is asking the City Commission to ratify and waive the competitive procurement requirements of Section 2-58 of the City code and authorize payment to DMS.

description:
The 6th cycle of Broward County transportation surtax projects is expected to begin soon. While we have no official notification of the timeline, we want to be prepared for a short deadline. If the Program continues as it has previously, up to three projects may be submitted. The City's approved Transportation Master Plan provides several projects from which to choose for funding, but two are the logical choices for this cycle.
In the 5th cycle (2023-2024), the City was awarded funding for a project to study ways to realign the 5 Points intersection to make it safer for pedestrians and bicyclists. Currently, FDOT is leading a multi-agency review of current conditions, and expects that process to be completed later this year. Once design is completed, we would want to proceed with construction of the proposed changes. A separate application is required for the construction phase and would be a top priority.
In addition to the 5 Points project, city staff recommends the improvements recommended in the TMP for Dixie Highway south of Five Points be considered for a surtax application in this upcoming cycle.
title: Discussion and possible direction on applying for 6th cycle Transportation Surtax Program and project selection

The Updated Plan shows clearly the progress the cities have made in achieving the goals of the original plan, while providing some aspirational proposed actions for the next five years.

attachments.name: 2025-009 RESO - Urging Florida Legislature to enact Public Records Exemption for Municipal Clerks

description: Currently, Florida Statute 119.071 provides exemptions for certain personal information of law enforcement personnel and other specific roles. However, municipal clerks and staff are not included in these exemptions, leaving their personal information vulnerable to public records requests. Municipal clerks and staff often handle sensitive information and perform critical administrative functions. Protecting their personal information is essential to ensure their safety. Many municipal staff who perform duties that include, or result in, investigations into complaints regarding election fraud, legal enforcement of hearings, proceedings related to violations of codes and ordinances, that could lead to a criminal prosecution, are exposed to threats and other acts of violence. Currently public records exemptions in Florida include those for local personnel who either investigate, enforce or otherwise provide a service that can result in contentious interactions when action is taken, and municipal clerks and their staff fall within the need for a window for greater protection.

description:
To ensure the City's Personnel and Safety Rules and Regulations are congruent with applicable laws and changing trends in employment practices, it is necessary to review the City's personnel policies on a periodic basis. The last revision to the Personnel Rules & Regulations was approved and instituted in September 2024. Approval of the recommended changes will afford the City and its employees a more comprehensive, current, and refined set of policies to which to adhere.
The following sections of the Personnel and Safety Rules and Regulations contain proposals for revisions to policy:
SECTION 7: Pay Plan
7-5: MIDPOINT AND TOP OUT PAY FOR EXEMPT EMPLOYEES
This is a new section
New language"An exempt employee who has been in the same management position for five (5) consecutive years will be placed at the midpoint of the designated pay range for their position, if they are not already at or above that salary amount. An exempt employee who has been in the same management position for ten (10) consecutive years will be placed at the top out pay range for their position, if they are not already at that salary amount.
Placing five (5) year and ten (10) year exempt employees at the midpoint and top out ensures they are being compensated at a competitive rate for their experience and performance.
Eligibility Criteria:The employee must remain in the same management position consecutively for the entire duration of the five (5) or ten (10) years. Same position means the employee must be in the same department in the exact same position for the entire duration of the five (5) or ten (10) years.If the employee changes departments or changes positions within their department, the required time period to qualify for a pay adjustment will reset.
If the employee’s title changes, but the position remains the same regarding job duties, functions, responsibilities and pay range, then the employee is eligible for midpoint or top out pay adjustments.
The employee must meet or exceed performance expectations as determined in their annual performance review for each qualifying year of the five (5) or ten (10) year period."
SECTION 8: Annual Leave
8-1: VACATION – REGULAR FULL-TIME EMPLOYEES
Edited subsection 3, creating three sections; a. General Employees, b. Exempt Employees and c. Department Directors, Assistant City Manager and City Manager.
Exempt Employees will begin employment with 4 weeks of vacation per year (accrual rate of .0770), which they will maintain through the first 5 years of employment. After 5 years of employment, they will receive the maximum of 5 weeks of vacation per year (accrual rate of .0961). Department Directors, Assistant City Manager and City Manager will receive 5 weeks of vacation per year (accrual rate of .0961).
These changes will impact all future qualifying employees and be awarded to all current qualifying employees, if they are not currently accruing at the new rate.
title: Motion to Approve Updates to the City's Personnel and Safety Rules and Regulations

description:
The City's code compliance unit processes are governed by FSS 162, Chapter 2 - Article III - Division 2 of our City's Code of Ordinances and department policy. These processes see officers issue Notices of Violation when violations of the City’s Code of Ordinances and Florida Building Code are identified, and violations not corrected within the required time are presented to, and ruled on, by the Special Magistrate. When compliance is not achieved in the timeframe ordered by the Special Magistrate, code liens are placed on properties within the City's jurisdiction. As of January 9, 2025, the City had 155 code liens attached to properties. The total amount of these liens was $11,774,735.00.
At the October 8, 2024 Commission meeting, staff was asked to construct a draft policy standardizing the City's lien foreclosure process, and to consider a lien amnesty program. Staff has conducted research in preparation for the Commission's discussion, and agenda item backup materials consist of the following: Memorandum with draft lien foreclosure policy standards, memorandum with draft lien amnesty program standards, master lien spreadsheet sorted by highest to lowest lien amounts, master lien spreadsheet sorted by TOC and A & E Zoning, master lien spreadsheet sorted by case number most recent to oldest, City zoning map, and information about other jurisdictions' lien amnesty programs. Staff has updated the lien records to show zoning districts and homesteaded properties.
Additionally, efforts have begun to again, notify property owners of the fact their property has a lien attached to it. Staff began with the top 10 highest lien amounts, and of these 10 properties, 6 remain in violation. Methods of contact used have been in person, and via letter mailed to the property owner and posting at the property. Staff stands ready to discuss this item and receive direction from the Commission.
title: Code Lien Foreclosure Policy and Lien Amnesty Program Discussion

description:
The owner of the property at the time of the violation, The OG Group LLC (Ori Darmon) was sent the first Notice of Violation on January 26, 2022, requesting compliance within fifteen (15) days, or the case would be brought to the Special Magistrate. The property was not brought into compliance, and the Special Magistrate hearing was set for July 13, 2022.
On July 13, 2022, the Special Magistrate heard Case 22-000157,which involved violations for failure to obtain the required permits for a home remodel and roof work at the property located at 209 NE 27 Drive. The property owner was granted additional time until August 13, 2022, to achieve compliance or face a fine of $250.00 per day. Routine inspections were completed on this property to seek voluntary compliance with negative results. Failure to achieve compliance within the allotted time prompted the case to be scheduled for the September 7, 2022, Special Magistrate Hearing.
On September 7, 2022, the Special Magistrate rendered an Order Certifying and Imposing Fine and Lien on the property.
On August 21, 2023, the property was brought into compliance. By that time, the property had remained in violation for a total of three hundred seventy-three (373) days at $250.00 per day, resulting in fines totaling $93,250.00.
On October 2, 2024, the Special Magistrate reduced the fine by 44% to $52,148.50, which is being appealed.
title: Appeal to Lien Reduction Order by Special Magistrate: Case 22-000157; 209 NE 27 Drive (Police)
